classification_signals: The present study assesses the effects of an architectural intervention on residential crowding stress and poststressor effects. (Abstract)

Residents of long-corridor, short-corridor, and long-corridor-intervention dormitory floors were surveyed and social behavior and space use patterns were systematically observed over a 3-month period. (Abstract)

Results section with subsections: Control, Group Formation, Crowding, Observational Findings, Laboratory Findings.
Statistical reporting (F-values, p-values) throughout the Results section.

limitations: The architectural intervention employed in this study should not be routinely extrapolated to other settings.
The direct applicability of interventions used in college dormitory environments to noncollege populations in other, larger scale environments must be seriously questioned.
It was not possible to survey all residents during orientation.

Attrition of subjects over the course of the semester was largely accounted for by illness or by scheduling problems; four students refused to complete subsequent questionnaires, two students moved to different dormitories, and eight were ill during the weeks that questionnaires were administered.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the effects of an architectural intervention on residential crowding stress and social behavior in college dormitories. By bisecting a long-corridor floor with a lounge area, the intervention reduced the effective group size from 40 to 20 residents. Findings indicated that residents of the modified long-corridor and short-corridor floors reported less crowding, greater perceived control, and more successful group formation compared to those in unaltered long-corridor floors. Observational data showed increased social activity and open doors in the intervention and short-corridor settings, while laboratory tasks revealed less withdrawal and greater persistence among residents of these environments. The study concludes that architectural design can mitigate crowding stress by facilitating group formation and control over social interaction. Limitations include concerns about generalizability to other settings and populations, and potential confounds, though the authors address some of these.

mechanism_chain.description: The architectural design of long-corridor dormitories restricts opportunities for social withdrawal, leading to increased unwanted social interaction and perceived crowding, which in turn contributes to residential social problems.
